Chapter 6 — Orthodontic Diagnosis: The Problem-Oriented Approach

The Diagnostic Database
  • Four issues must be faced in determining the optimal treatment plan: (1) the timing of treatment, (2) the complexity of the treatment that would be required, (3) the predictability of success with a given treatment approach, and (4) the patient's (and parents') goals and desires.
  • The problem-oriented approach to diagnosis and treatment planning has been widely advocated in medicine and dentistry as a way to overcome the tendency to concentrate on only one aspect of a patient's problems.
  • For orthodontic purposes, the database may be thought of as derived from three major sources:
    • Interview data from questions (written and oral) of the patient
    • Clinical examination of the patient
    • Evaluation of diagnostic records, including dental casts, radiographs, and photographs.
Questionnaire & Interview
  • The goals of the interview process are to establish the patient's chief concern; medical and dental history; physical growth status; motivation, expectations, and other social and behavioral factors.
Reorganized (7th) The 7th edition frames the interview as the chief concern plus two major areas: (1) medical and dental history; and (2) motivation, expectations and other factors — physical-growth status now sits in its own evaluation (below).

I Chief Concern

  • There are three major reasons for patient concern about the alignment and occlusion of the teeth: impaired dentofacial appearance, impaired function, and impaired oral health.

II Medical and Dental History

  • Three areas deserve a special comments:
    • First, although most children with a condylar fracture of the mandible recover uneventfully, a growth deficit related to an old injury is the most probable cause of true facial asymmetry.
    • Second, whether the patient is on long-term medication of any type and, if so, for what purpose.
    • Third, many children and adults now survive serious illness and seek orthodontic treatment afterward.
      • Cancer chemotherapy and radiation therapy aimed at head and neck tissues can result in morphologic impacts such as short roots or missing teeth.
      • In adults being treated for arthritis or osteoporosis, and now increasingly also in children with acute and chronic disease treated with drugs (such as glucocorticoids) that can be toxic to bone, high doses of resorption-inhibiting agents such as bisphosphonates often are used. This impedes orthodontic tooth movement and may increase the chance of complications.

III Physical Growth Evaluation

  • The stage of dental development should not be used to estimate the stage of jaw growth, that correlates less well with skeletal growth than almost any other developmental index.
  • Unfortunately, the stage of vertebral development is less useful in establishing whether jaw growth has subsided to adult levels in a teenager with mandibular prognathism. Hand‒wrist radiographs are an alternative method for evaluating skeletal maturity, but these also are not an accurate way to determine when growth is completed. Serial cephalometric radiographs offer the most accurate way to determine whether facial growth has stopped or is continuing.
Renamed & expanded (7th) This section is now "Statural and Sexual Maturation Evaluation." The 7th adds that if you record height you should use a reliable method — the stadiometer (a wall-mounted ruler with a sliding horizontal measuring arm); done without attention to detail, more than 50% of measures are inaccurate.

IV Social and Behavioral Evaluation

  • Motivation for seeking treatment can be classified as external (pressure from another individual) or internal.
  • Older patients usually are aware of psychosocial difficulties or functional problems related to their malocclusion and so are likely to have some component of internal motivation.
  • Cooperation is more likely to be a problem with a child than an adult. Two factors are important in determining this:
    • The extent to which the child sees the treatment as a benefit, as opposed to something else he or she is required to undergo
    • The degree of parental control or parenting style. (The best cooperation with treatment most probably will be achieved with authoritative (not authoritarian) parents who will be demanding but responsive to their children.
  • Treating an unwilling child, even if the parents force an apparent assent, rarely is good judgment.
Clinical Evaluation
  • Two goals of the orthodontic clinical examination:
    1. Evaluate and document oral health, jaw function, facial proportions, and smile characteristics
    2. Decide which diagnostic records are required.

I Oral Health

  • The general guideline is that before orthodontic treatment begins, any disease or pathologic condition must be under control.
  • In the periodontal evaluation, there are two major points of interest: indications of active periodontal disease, and potential or actual mucogingival problems.
  • Aggressive juvenile periodontitis occurs rarely, but if it is present, it is critically important to note this before orthodontic treatment begins.
  • Inadequate attached gingiva around crowded incisors may lead to stripping of the gingiva away from the teeth when the teeth are aligned, especially if the dental arch is expanded.
  • Teeth with developmental defects of morphology and hard tissue quality are more susceptible to decalcification and decay during treatment, extraction of a defective tooth rather than a sound one should be considered when extractions are part of the plan.
New data & treatments (7th) The 7th edition adds that white spot lesions in orthodontic patients have an incidence of nearly 46% and a prevalence of 68%; highly-rated managements include self-assembling peptide (SAP) P11-4 with fluoride varnish and resin infiltration. It also names Molar Incisor Hypomineralization (MIH) — demarcated enamel opacities, reported in 12%–20% of children — as a pre-existing esthetic issue to flag.

II Jaw and Occlusal Function

  • Four aspects of oral function require evaluation: mastication (including swallowing), speech, the possibility of sleep apnea related to mandibular deficiency, and the presence or absence of TMJ problems.
  • Mastication:
    • Unfortunately, there are almost no reasonable diagnostic tests to evaluate masticatory efficiency.
    • Swallowing is almost never affected by malocclusion. (Juvenile swallowing pattern and open bite?)
    • Oral gymnastic tests (such as measuring lip strength or how hard the patient can push with the tongue) add little or nothing to the diagnostic evaluation.
  • Speech:
    • Speech problems can be related to malocclusion, but normal speech is possible in the presence of severe anatomic distortions. Table 6.1.
    • If a child has a speech problem and the type of malocclusion related to it, a combination of speech therapy and orthodontics may help.
  • Sleep Apnea:
    • Both the diagnosis and management of sleep disorders requires an interdisciplinary team and should not be attempted without assessment, documentation, and referral from a qualified physician.
    • Oral appliances to advance the mandible can be effective, but only in patients with mild sleep apnea.
  • TMJ:
    • The most important indicators of joint function are the amount of maximum opening and the ability of the mandible to translate beyond the hinge movement.
    • Palpating the muscles of mastication and TMJs should be a routine part of any dental examination.
    • Children with an apparent unilateral crossbite often have a bilateral narrowing of the maxillary arch, with a shift to the unilateral crossbite position. This is the most common cause of apparent but not true facial asymmetry.
    • Many children and adults with a Class II malocclusion and an underlying skeletal Class II jaw relationship will position the mandible forward in a "Sunday bite", making the occlusion look better than it really is.
    • Sometimes an apparent Class III relationship results from a forward shift to escape incisor interferences in what is really an end-to-end relationship Fig 6.8. Called pseudo–Class III malocclusion.
    • Balancing interferences, presence or absence of canine protection in lateral excursions, and other such factors take on greater significance if they are still present when the occlusal changes produced by orthodontic treatment are nearing completion.
Restructured (7th) The 7th lists only three aspects of oral function here — mastication, speech, and TMJ — because sleep apnea is moved out to its own screening section (your summary, from the 6th, lists four with sleep apnea included).
New — sleep-apnea screening (7th) A major new section: obstructive sleep apnea has a prevalence of up to 5% in children and 9%–38% of adults. Validated screening questionnaires are added — the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ, 22 items) for children and STOP-Bang for adults. The polysomnogram is the gold standard for diagnosis; severity is the Apnea–Hypopnea Index (AHI): in children <1 event/h is normal; in adults <5 is normal, 5–15 mild, 15–30 moderate, >30 severe.

III Facial and Dental Appearance

  • Systematic Examination of Facial and Dental Appearance:
    1. Facial proportions in all three planes of space (macro-esthetics).
    2. The dentition in relation to the face "smile" (mini-esthetics).
    3. The teeth in relation to one another (micro-esthetics).
New framing (7th) The 7th retitles this "The Evolution to Today's Soft-Tissue Paradigm" and adds a history — the paradigm traces to Norman Kingsley and the Angle school, which even brought in art professor Dr. Edmund Wuerpel to teach Greco-Roman proportion. It also quantifies (Papio et al, 2019) how much facial attractiveness the teeth contribute: there is a clear interaction between facial and dental attractiveness, judged differently for males and females, so both the facial and the dental attractiveness of the patient must be assessed.

Macro-Esthetics: Facial Proportions

  • Assessment of Developmental Age: The degree of physical development is much more important than chronologic age in determining how much growth remains.
  • Facial Esthetics Vs Facial Proportions
  • Frontal Examination: (in short, exclude syndromes and asymmetry, establish facial proportions)
    • Frontal examination is the first step in analyzing facial proportions
    • Low-set ears or eyes that are unusually far apart (hypertelorism) may indicate either the presence of a syndrome or a microform of a craniofacial anomaly. If a syndrome is suspected, the patient's hands should be examined for syndactyly, because there are several dental‒digital syndromes.
    • Bilateral symmetry in the fifths of the face and for proportionality of the widths of the eyes, nose, and mouth Fig 6.9. A small degree of bilateral facial asymmetry exists in essentially all normal individuals.
    • "Normal asymmetry" usually results from a small size difference between the two sides, should be distinguished from a chin or nose that deviates to one side.
    • The proportional relationship of facial height to width (the facial index) establishes the overall facial type and the basic proportions of the face.
    • It is important to note the cause of vertical problems such as excessive display of the maxillary gingiva, which is done best by examining the position of lips and teeth relative to the vertical thirds of the face Fig 6.14.
  • Profile Analysis: (in short, facial AP relationship, lip posture, vertical proportions "mandibular angle")
    1. Establishing whether the jaws are proportionately positioned in the anteroposterior (AP) plane
      • Requires placing the patient in the physiologic natural head position (NHP)
      • Facial angle (convex, straight, concave). These line segments ideally should form a nearly straight line, with only a slight inclination in either direction. A large angle between them (>10 degrees or so) indicates either profile convexity or profile concavity.
    2. Evaluation of lip posture and incisor prominence.
      • The teeth protrude excessively if (and only if) two conditions are met:
        • (1) The lips are prominent and everted
        • (2) the lips are separated at rest by more than 3 to 4 mm (lip incompetence).
      • If the lips are prominent but close over the teeth without strain, the lip posture is largely independent of tooth position. For that individual, retracting the incisor teeth would have little effect on lip function or prominence.
      • In evaluating lip protrusion, it is important to keep in mind that everything is relative (the lip relationships with the nose and chin affect the perception of lip fullness). The larger the nose, the more prominent the chin must be to balance it, and the greater the amount of lip prominence that will be esthetically acceptable.
      • Some patients with short lower face height have everted and protrusive lips because they are overclosed and the upper lip presses against the lower lip, not because the teeth protrude. One indicator of lip protrusion caused by overclosure is the labiomental fold angulation. Under normal conditions this is usually somewhat obtuse; a greatly decreased angle indicates overclosure.
    3. Re-evaluation of vertical facial proportions and evaluation of mandibular plane angle.
      • Vertical proportions can be observed during the full-face examination but sometimes can be seen more clearly in profile.
      • The inclination of the mandibular plane to the true horizontal should be noted.
New — facial form analysis (7th) Taken together, this clinical (no-radiography) macroesthetic evaluation is now named the facial form analysis, and the 7th gives explicit profile→skeletal rules — e.g. a convex profile with Class II molars and >5 mm overjet = a skeletal Class II (and Class I with 2–5 mm overjet, Class III with 0/negative overjet), extending the dental classification to the skeleton.

Mini-Esthetics: Tooth–Lip Relationship and Smile Analysis

  • Symmetry: the relationship of the dental midline of each arch to the skeletal midline of that jaw. Table 6.6
  • Vertical relationship of the teeth to the lips at rest and on smile.
    • For patients with excessive incisor display, the usual cause is a long lower third of the face, but that is not the only possibility; a short upper lip could produce the same thing.
  • Up‒down transverse rotation of the dentition
    • Often is called a transverse cant of the occlusal plane
    • Dentists detect a transverse roll at 1 mm from side to side, whereas laypersons are more forgiving and see it at 2 to 3 mm
  • Smile analysis
    • There are two types of smiles: the posed or social smile and the enjoyment smile (Duchenne smile).
    • The social smile is reasonably reproducible, and it is the focus of orthodontic diagnosis.
    • Amount of incisor and gingival display:
      • The ideal elevation of the lip on smile for adolescents is slightly below the gingival margin with 2 mm of tooth coverage
      • More important, the acceptable range of tooth display is from minimal tooth coverage of 1 mm up to 4 mm coverage of the incisor crown. Beyond that, the smile appearance is less attractive.
      • 1 to 2 mm of gingival display, is the maximum acceptable amount on a social smile.
    • Transverse dimensions of the smile relative to the upper arch. (Buccal corridors) Fig 6.26
    • The smile arch (The contour of the incisal edges should parallel the curvature of the lower lip)

Micro-Esthetics: Close-up Dental Appearance

  • Tooth proportions
    • Width Relationships and the "Golden Proportion." Fig 6.29
    • Height‒Width Relationships. Fig 6.30
    • Connectors and Embrasures. Fig 6.31
    • Embrasures: Black Triangles.
  • Gingival height, shape, and contour Fig 6.33.
    • The central incisor has the highest gingival level (along with canine), the lateral incisor is approximately 1.5 mm lower.
    • Gingival shape refers to the curvature of the gingiva at the margin of the tooth. For best appearance, the gingival shape of the maxillary lateral incisors should be a symmetric half-oval or half-circle. The maxillary centrals and canines should exhibit a gingival shape that is more elliptical and oriented distally to the long axis of the tooth
    • The gingival zenith (the most apical point of the gingival tissue) should be located distal to the longitudinal axis of the maxillary centrals and canines; the gingival zenith of the maxillary laterals should coincide with their longitudinal axis.
  • Tooth shade and color
    • A normal progression of shade change from the midline posteriorly is an important contributor to an attractive and natural-appearing smile. The maxillary central incisors tend to be the brightest in the smile, the lateral incisors less so, and the canines the least bright. First and second premolars are more closely matched to the lateral incisors.
Diagnostic Records

I Which Diagnostic Records are Needed

  • Orthodontic records fall into the same three major categories used for development of the diagnostic database: those for evaluation of the (1) health of the teeth and oral structures, (2) alignment and occlusal relationships of the teeth, and (3) facial and jaw proportions
  • Records for Health of Teeth and Oral Structure
    • A major purpose of intraoral photographs.
    • Current guidelines for radiographs (for pathologic conditions) Table 6.8
    • The panoramic image has two significant advantages over a series of intraoral radiographs: It yields a broader view and the radiation exposure is much lower. It also gives a view of the mandibular condyles, which can be helpful.
    • The principle is that periapical or other radiographs to supplement the panoramic radiograph are ordered only if there is a specific indication for doing so.
  • Dental Records
    • Evaluation of the occlusion requires two things: impressions for dental casts or digital scanning, and a record of the occlusion (either a wax bite or a buccal scan)
    • Articulator Mounting, There are three reasons for mounting casts on articulators:
      1. Record and document any discrepancy between the occlusal relations at the initial contact of the teeth and the relations at the patient's full or habitual occlusion. (functional shift)
      2. Record the lateral and excursive paths of the mandible.
      3. Display the orientation of the occlusal plane to the face. (which is superseded by CBCT images)
    • In adults with symptoms of temporomandibular dysfunction, articulator-mounted casts may be useful to document significant discrepancies between habitual and relaxed mandibular positions.
    • Articulators are indicated for adult patients with functional problems, not for children or adolescents.
  • Records for Dentofacial Proportions
    • Radiographs:
      • Lateral cephalometric radiographs are the standard for comprehensive orthodontic treatment. Like all radiographic records, cephalograms should be taken only when they are indicated.
      • The major indication for a frontal (posteroanterior [PA], not AP) cephalometric radiograph was facial asymmetry, and this now is an indication for 3-D imaging instead.
      • As general rules: If you have the panoramic radiograph and there is a suspected localized issue, you will best serve the patient in terms of radiation by getting a cephalometric radiograph and a small-field CBCT view, because you will likely need higher resolution of the problem area. If none of these images are available and you need a panoramic, cephalometric radiograph and a close-up view of a specific localized area, a full-field image can address all these issues, although the panoramic and cephalometric radiographs constructed from CBCT have lower resolution than individual images.
    • Facial photographs:
      • The minimum set is three photographs, frontal at rest, frontal smile, and profile at rest.
      • The oblique smiling photo, for instance, provides an excellent view of both vertical tooth‒lip relationships and the smile arc.
Updated guidance (7th) The radiograph selection guidelines were revised in 2012, and the 7th adds the ABO recommendation that pretreatment radiographs for adults (>18 yr) include a panoramic, bitewings, and periapical radiographs. Radiation risk is now communicated in mSv against the ~3.1 mSv average annual US background dose, with cancer risk estimated at 5.5%/Sv (ICRP No. 103).

II Analysis of Diagnostic Records

  • The focus is on four things:
    1. Dental cast analysis to evaluate symmetry and space analysis.
    2. Cephalometric analysis of dentofacial relationships
    3. Analysis of 3-D CBCT images
    4. Integration of information from all sources into the problem-oriented format

Cast Analysis: Symmetry, Space, and Tooth Size

  • Symmetry:
    • Asymmetry within the dental arch but with a symmetric arch form can occur. This is due either to severe crowding or spacing or to drift of anterior or posterior teeth on one side of the arch.
  • Alignment, Crowding, and Spacing: Space Analysis.
  • Tooth Size Analysis:
    • 5% of the population have some degree tooth size discrepancy.
    • Variation in the upper lateral incisors (enlarged, or peg-shaped) is the most common cause.
    • Tooth size analysis (Bolton analysis). A tooth size discrepancy of less than 1.5 mm is rarely significant, but larger discrepancies create treatment problems in achieving ideal occlusion.

Cephalometric Analysis

  • Measurement Analysis
  • Choice of a Horizontal (Cranial) Reference Line:
    • An international congress of anatomists and physical anthropologists was held in Frankfort, in 1882. At the conference, the Frankfort plane, was adopted as the best representation of the natural orientation of the skull, because it was often parallel to the true horizontal when people were standing in a relaxed position.
    • The Frankfort plane has two difficulties:
      • The first is that both its anterior and posterior landmarks, particularly porion, can be difficult to locate reliably on a cephalometric radiograph.
        • "machine porion," is often used to locate porion. The upper edge of this canal can also be used to establish "anatomic porion," which gives a slightly different Frankfort plane
        • An alternative horizontal reference line (SN) (6 to 7 degrees upward anteriorly to the Frankfort plane)
      • The second problem is more fundamental. Everyone orients his or her head in a characteristic position, which is established physiologically, not anatomically. In most patients the true horizontal line closely approximates the Frankfort plane. Some individuals, however, show significant differences, up to 10 degrees.
    • For living patients, however, it is possible to use a "true horizontal" line, established physiologically rather than anatomically, as the horizontal reference plane (line perpendicular to the true vertical) Fig 6.51.
  • Steiner Analysis: (ANB / SN-MP / U1 to NA, L1 to NB angular & mm)
    • Developed and promoted by Cecil Steiner in the 1950s
    • Steiner analysis can be considered the first of the modern cephalometric analyses for two reasons:
      • It displayed measurements in a way that emphasized not just the individual measurements but their interrelationship in a pattern
      • It offered specific guides for use of cephalometric measurements in treatment planning.
    • Steiner analysis was based on evaluating the compensations necessary to compensate for the difference between SNA and SNB (dental compensations of the skeletal jaw discrepancy) Fig 6.52.
    • The ANB angle was the measurement of real interest. One can argue, that which jaw is at fault is of mostly theoretical interest; what really matters is the magnitude of the discrepancy.
    • The more prominent the chin, the more prominent the incisor can be, and vice versa. This important relationship is often referred to as the Holdaway ratio.
    • Steiner measured the angular and millimeter relationship of the upper incisor to the NA line and both the lower incisor and the chin to the NB line, thus establishing the relative protrusion of the dentition Fig 6.53.
    • Another important measurement included in Steiner analysis is the inclination of the mandibular plane to SN, which is its only indicator of the vertical proportions.
    • There were significant problems with the Steiner analysis:
      • First, its reliance on ANB is problematic. The ANB angle is influenced by two factors other than the AP difference in jaw position:
        • As the vertical distance between nasion and points A and B increases, the ANB angle will decrease.
        • If the AP position of the nasion is abnormal, the size of the angle will be affected.
      • Second, relying on tooth movement alone to correct skeletal malocclusion, particularly as the skeletal discrepancies become large, is not necessarily the best approach to orthodontic treatment.
  • Sassouni Analysis:
    • The first to emphasize vertical, as well as horizontal, relationships and the interaction between vertical and horizontal proportions. Fig 6.54.
    • Sassouni pointed out that the horizontal anatomic planes (Frankfort plane, palatal plane, occlusal plane, and mandibular plane) tend to converge toward a single point in well-proportioned faces. The inclination of these planes to each other reflects the vertical proportionality of the face.
    • Sassouni coined the term skeletal open bite and skeletal deep bite.
  • Harvold and Wits Analysis:
    • Both analyses are aimed solely at describing the severity or degree of jaw disharmony.
    • Harvold developed standards for the "unit length" of the maxilla and mandible. and lower face height Fig 6.55
    • The position of the teeth has no influence on the Harvold figures.
    • Wits analysis was conceived primarily as a way to overcome the limitations of ANB as an indicator of jaw discrepancy.
    • It is important for Wits analysis to use the functional occlusal plane, drawn along the maximum intercuspation of the posterior teeth, not the Downs analysis functional plane influenced by the vertical position of the incisors.
  • McNamara Analysis:
    • Combines elements of previous approaches (Ricketts and Harvold) with original measurements to attempt a more precise definition of jaw and tooth positions. Fig 6.56
    • The AP position of the maxilla and mandible are evaluated with regard to their position relative to the "nasion perpendicular," a vertical line extending downward from nasion perpendicular to the Frankfort plane.
    • The lower incisor is related as in the Ricketts analysis, primarily by using the A-pogonion line.
    • The McNamara analysis has two major strengths:
      • First, it relates the jaws via the true vertical line. (Using a true vertical line, perpendicular to the true horizontal rather than anatomic Frankfort, would be better)
      • Second, the normative data are based on the well-defined Bolton sample (Bolton growth study) "highly compatible with preliminary analysis by comparison with the Bolton templates".
  • Counterpart Analysis:
    • Major problem with any analysis based on individual measurements is that any one dimension is affected by others within the same face.
    • The basic idea of interrelated vertical and horizontal dimensions leading to an ultimately balanced or unbalanced facial pattern was first expressed by Enlow et al in a "counterpart analysis".
    • The idea is to use standards derived from the individual's facial type rather than relating individual cephalometric values to population means (correlations among the individual values). Fig 6.57
  • Template Analysis:
    • In recent years, direct comparison of patients with templates derived from the various growth studies has become a reliable method of analysis, with two major advantages:
      • Compensatory skeletal and dental deviations within an individual can be observed directly
      • Changes in dimensions with changing ages can be evaluated by using age-appropriate templates.
    • Templates of this type have been prepared by using the data from the major growth studies.
    • Templates exist in two forms: schematic (show the changing position of selected landmarks with age on a single template) and anatomically complete "Bolton" (a different one for each age, are particularly convenient for direct visual comparison of a patient with the reference group while accounting for age)
    • Bolton templates are most often used for template analysis.
    • Analysis using a template is based on a series of superimpositions of the template over a tracing of the patient being analyzed. The sequence of superimpositions follows:
      1. Cranial base superimposition, maxilla and mandible to the cranium Fig 6.58.
      2. Maxillary superimposition. Superimposition on the maximum contour of the maxilla to evaluate the relationship of the maxillary dentition to the maxilla Fig 6.59.
      3. Mandibular superimposition. Superimposition on the symphysis of the mandible to evaluate the relationship of the mandibular dentition to the mandible Fig 6.60.
    • Template analysis in this fashion quickly provides an overall impression of the way in which the patient's dentofacial structures are related.
  • Cephalometric Methodology in a Digital Age
    • It is important to follow a sequence of steps in cephalometric analysis:
      1. Look carefully at the overall image for pathologic issues
      2. Look for head positioning errors if there are indications of asymmetry. If the structures in the upper part of the image (e.g., orbits, key ridges, greater wings of the sphenoid) are evenly spaced and those in the lower part are not (or vice versa), that usually indicates skeletal asymmetry.
      3. Check the landmark points.
      4. Look for consistency in similar types of measures.
      5. Look for facial proportionality or lack of it.
  • Three-Dimensional Imaging in Modern Orthodontics (CBCT)
    • Basic Concepts
      • Two types of image resolution are important: contrast resolution, the ability to distinguish between tissues of different densities (somewhat limited because CBCT images have low soft tissue contrast), and spatial resolution, the ability to distinguish between separate structures that are positioned very close together.
    • Orthodontic Applications of CBCT — Four situations in which enough data now exist to support use of CBCT for orthodontic patients:
      1. Ectopically Erupting or Impacted Teeth.
      2. Facial Asymmetry and Complex Orthognathic Surgery.
      3. Congenital Deformities, Syndromes, and Facial Trauma.
      4. Hard Tissue Aspects of Temporomandibular Joint Problems.
Orthodontic Classification

I Development of Classification Systems

  • The first useful orthodontic classification was Angle's classification of malocclusion into Classes I, II, and III.
  • Angle's classification numbers were extended to refer to four distinct but related characteristics: the classification of malocclusion; the molar relationship; the skeletal jaw relationship; and the pattern of growth Fig 6.73.
  • In the 1960s, Ackerman and Proffit formalized the system of informal additions to the Angle method by identifying five major characteristics of malocclusion to be considered and systematically described in classification Fig 6.74.
  • The approach overcame the major weaknesses of the Angle scheme.
    • Incorporated an evaluation of crowding and asymmetry within the dental arches and incisor protrusion.
    • Recognized the relationship between protrusion and crowding.
    • Included the transverse and vertical, as well as the AP, planes of space
    • Incorporated information about skeletal jaw proportions at the appropriate point.
  • Experience has confirmed that a minimum of five characteristics must be considered in a complete diagnosis.
  • The most important change, is the greater emphasis now on evaluating facial soft tissue proportions and the relationship of the dentition to the lips and cheeks, on smile and at rest.

II Additions to the Five-Characteristics Classification System

  • Two things particularly help this more thorough analysis:
  • Esthetic line of the dentition:
    • Angle's concept was that if the buccal occlusal line of the mandibular dental arch was coincident with the central fossae line of the maxillary dental arch and the teeth were well aligned, ideal occlusion would result.
    • In modern analysis, another curved line characterizing the appearance of the dentition is important, the one that is seen when evaluating anterior tooth display Fig 6.75. This line, the esthetic line of the dentition, follows the facial edges of the maxillary anterior and posterior teeth.
  • Pitch, roll, and yaw in systematic description:
    • A complete description, requires consideration of both translation in 3-D space and rotation about three perpendicular axes (pitch, roll, and yaw) Fig 6.76.
    • Evaluating pitch, roll, and yaw of the esthetic line of the dentition is particularly useful in determining the relationship of the teeth to the soft tissues that frame their display.
  • Pitch: Fig 6.77
    • An excessive upward‒downward rotation of the dentition relative to the lips and cheeks would be noted as pitch (up or down, in front or back).
    • Pitch of the dentition relative to the facial soft tissues must be evaluated on clinical examination. "gingival display"
    • Pitch of the jaws and teeth relative to each other and to the facial skeleton should be noted clinically, but this can be confirmed from the cephalometric radiograph where pitch is revealed as the orientation of the palatal, occlusal, and mandibular planes relative to the true horizontal.
  • Roll: Fig 6.78
    • Described as rotation up or down on one side or the other. On clinical examination, it is important to relate the transverse orientation of the dentition (the esthetic line) to both the facial soft tissues and the facial skeleton. "occlusal canting"
    • The relationship to the facial soft tissues is evaluated clinically with the intercommissure line as a reference, in both frontal and oblique views
    • The relationship to the facial skeleton is viewed relative to the interocular line.
  • Yaw: Fig 6.79
    • Rotation of the jaw or dentition to one side or the other, around a vertical axis, produces a skeletal or dental midline discrepancy.
    • The effect of yaw, in addition to dental and/or skeletal midline deviations, typically is a unilateral Class II or Class III molar relationship. Extreme yaw is associated with asymmetric posterior crossbites, buccal on one side and lingual on the other.
    • Dental midline deviations can be just a reflection of displaced incisors because of crowding. This should be differentiated from a yaw discrepancy in which the whole dental arch is rotated.

III Classification by the Characteristics of Malocclusion

  • Step 1: Evaluation of Facial Proportions and Esthetics
    • Facial asymmetry, AP and vertical facial proportions, and lip‒tooth relationships (at rest and on smile) are evaluated. This also includes evaluating whether a cant to the dentition exists (Macro- and Mini-esthetics)
  • Step 2: Evaluation of Alignment and Symmetry Within the Dental Arches
    • Evaluating first the symmetry within each dental arch and second the amount of crowding or spacing.
    • A major point is the presence or absence of excessive incisor protrusion, which cannot be evaluated without knowledge of lip separation at rest. For that reason, the dentofacial relationships noted in the initial clinical examination must be considered along with the relationship of the teeth to the line of occlusion.
  • Step 3: Evaluation of the Transverse Plane of Space
    • Casts are brought into occlusion and the occlusal relationships are examined, beginning with the transverse (posterior crossbite) plane of space. Fig 6.80
    • Both roll and yaw of the jaws and dentition affect dentofacial transverse relationships.
    • Bilateral maxillary lingual (or palatal) crossbite means that the upper molars are lingual to their normal position on both sides, whereas a unilateral mandibular buccal crossbite would mean that the mandibular molars are buccally positioned on one side.
  • Step 4: Evaluation of the Anteroposterior Plane of Space
    • Whether an end-to-end, Class II or Class III buccal segment relationship, or excessive overjet or reverse overjet of the incisors, is caused by a jaw (skeletal) discrepancy, (dental Class II or III), or a combination.
    • If the jaw discrepancy is the cause, the problem should be described as a skeletal Class II or Class III.
    • Cephalometric analysis is needed to be precise about the nature of the problem.
    • Occasionally the molar occlusion is Class II on one side and Class I on the other. Angle called this a Class II subdivision, right or left. In modern classification, the subdivision label rarely is useful because it does not describe the real problem. The asymmetric molar relationship reflects either an asymmetry within one or both the dental arches (typically due to loss of space when one primary second molar was lost prematurely) or a yaw discrepancy of the jaw or dentition.
  • Step 5: Evaluation of the Vertical Plane of Space
    • Vertical problems can be described as anterior open bite, anterior deep bite, or posterior open bite.
    • If the posterior teeth erupt a normal amount but the anterior teeth do not, there will be a pitch discrepancy of the line of occlusion and the esthetic line of the dentition.
Development of a Problem List
  • The problem list often includes two types of problems: those relating to disease or pathologic processes and those relating to disturbances of development that have created the patient's malocclusion.
  • When possible, the problems should be indicated quantitatively or at least classified as mild, moderate, or severe.
